newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan advises India against pre-empting groups.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan advises India against pre-empting groups.

text.p: Pakistan, angered by India's apparent restaking of its claim on disputed Kashmir, urged New Delhi on Thursday to avoid prejudicing the task of proposed working groups for peace.

The two arch-rival Asian neighbours battled verbally only three days after agreeing on an agenda for future peace talks, including the dispute over the Himalayan region of Kashmir, and on avoiding hostile propaganda against each other.

The row was sparked by Indian Foreign Ministry Secretary Salman Haider's statement on Wednesday that New Delhi wanted to focus on what he called Pakistani military "occupation" of part of Kashmir rather than the legitimacy of its own rule in the region that Islamabad questions.
"Well, we are a little disappointed," a Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesman said on Thursday about Haider's remarks at a news conference in New Delhi on Wednewday.
A joint statement issued on Monday after talks between Haider and his Pakistani counterpart Shamshad Ahmad listed eight issues to be tackled by working groups that have yet to be formed.

Topping the list was peace and security, including undefined confidence-building measures, followed by disputes over Kashmir, the Siachen glacier in Kashmir, Wullar Barrage project in India-ruled Kashmir, and Sir Creek estuary on the Arabian Sea.
Other issues are terrorism and drug trafficking, economic and cultural cooperation, and promotion of friendly exchanges.

Talks on confidence-building between the two potential nuclear powers, military analysts say, could span mutual reduction of forces and defence budgets, agreements on non-production of nuclear weapons and non-deployment of missiles against each other.
On the main Kashmir dispute, India, which rules two-thirds of the Himalayan region, lays claim to all of the region.
Islamabad, which controls the remaining third, wants the predominantly Moslem Kashmiris to decide in a U.N.-mandated plebiscite on whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.
Some Kashmiri groups fighting Indian rule since a rebellion erupted in 1990 want to reunite Kashmir as an independent state.

The confrontation on Siachen glacier, 76 km (47 miles) long and from two km (1.25 miles) to eight km (five miles) wide, began in 1984 with the two sides moving troops there for the first time in an area where a line of control dividing the rest of Kashmir was not demarcated.
More soldiers have been killed by harsh weather than in combat on the 20,000-foot (6,100-metre) high Siachen, the world's highest battlefield.

India says the Wullar barrage, also known as the Tulbul navigation project, is designed to solve a navigation problem over a distance of about 20 km (12 miles) from Wullar lake to Baramula town in the Kashmir Valley.
Pakistan objects, saying this is the work not of navigation control but of storage in breach of a 1960 river water distribution treaty between the two countries.

On Sir Creek, India asserts that the boundary lies in the middle of the 96-km (60-mile) long estuary in the marshes of the Rann of Kutch, where demarcation was left out of an arbitration tribunal's award in 1968 after armed clashes in 1965.
Pakistan says the boundary lies on the creek's eastern bank on the Indian side and, therefore, the entire waterway belongs to Islamabad.
